theme: I cry aloud to God; I remember your wonders of old
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 77. It begins in distress and ends with a picture of the exodus. Read it aloud, and notice the exact moment when the psalmist turns from his own trouble to God’s past deeds.
settingTheScene: Psalm 77 was written by Asaph, who also wrote Psalm 73. Like that one, it is the prayer of a person whose faith is shaken. But where Psalm 73 turned on the sanctuary, this psalm turns on memory. The psalmist faces a time of such trouble that he cannot sleep. And then he remembers the exodus, which you have just read. The psalm shows how the story of redemption is meant to be used: as a resource for hard days.
observation: “I cry aloud to God, aloud to God, and he will hear me” (v. 1).
“In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord; in the night my hand is stretched out without wearying; my soul refuses to be comforted” (v. 2).
“When I remember God, I am distressed; when I meditate, my spirit faints” (v. 3).
“You hold my eyelids open; I am so troubled that I cannot speak” (v. 4).
He asks a series of questions: “Will the Lord spurn forever…? Has his steadfast love forever ceased? Has God forgotten to be gracious?” (vv. 7-9).
Then, “I will appeal to this, to the years of the right hand of the Most High” (v. 10).
“I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old” (v. 11).
“Your way, O God, is holy. What god is great like our God? You are the God who works wonders” (vv. 13-14).
“With your arm you redeemed your people, the children of Jacob and Joseph” (v. 15).
“Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen” (v. 19). “You led your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron” (v. 20).
interpretation:
The first nine verses of this psalm are a portrait of spiritual distress, and it is worth noticing what is unusual about it. “When I remember God, I am distressed.” You might expect that remembering God would be comforting. Here it is painful, because the psalmist remembers what God has been, and compares it to what he feels now. It is the distress of someone who believes in a good God and cannot reconcile that with his experience.

The questions of verses 7 to 9 are the real question at the heart of the psalm. Will the Lord reject forever? Has his steadfast love ceased? Has he forgotten? Each question is a way of asking whether the covenant is still good. And the psalmist does not answer them right away.

The turn comes in verse 10. “Then I said, I will appeal to this.” The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and translations vary, but the sense is that the psalmist makes a decision. He will stop focusing on his feelings, and he will recall what God has done. “I will remember the deeds of the LORD.” This is a deliberate act of the will. He does not wait to feel like remembering.

What does he remember? The exodus. Verses 16 to 20 are a lyrical retelling of the crossing of the sea. The waters trembled. The depths shook. The clouds poured out water. God’s arrows and thunder flashed. The picture is of a storm, and God is at the center of it. And then the line that is the most striking of all: “Your way was through the sea…yet your footprints were unseen.” God’s way was through the sea, but you could not see his tracks. This is a profound description of providence. God was at work, with absolute power, but invisibly. There were no footprints.

That is the answer to the psalmist’s problem. His circumstances do not show God’s footprints, but that does not mean that God is not at work. The exodus proved that God can lead his people through impossible places without leaving a visible trace. And the psalm ends with the quiet image of a shepherd: “You led your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.” He leads through human hands, and he leads like a shepherd.
connection: Paul writes in Romans 11:33 about God’s “paths beyond tracing out.” Jesus asked his disciples to remember the feeding of the five thousand when they worried about bread (Mark 8:17-21). At the Lord’s Supper, Jesus told his followers, “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). Psalm 77’s pattern, of distress, then deliberate remembering, then worship, is also the pattern in Psalm 42 and Lamentations 3.
application:
When your feelings are overwhelming, remember on purpose. Write out a list of the deeds of the LORD in your life, and in the Bible. Read it aloud.

Think about a time you could not see God’s footprints, and later saw that he had been working. Tell someone about it.

Take the Lord’s Supper as an act of remembering, not only as a ritual.
prayerPrompts: Cry out to God, and tell him where your soul refuses to be comforted.
Remember aloud a deed of God that you can hold on to.
Thank him that he leads you even when you cannot see his footprints.
